analysis.one_liner: Funds more federal wage-and-hour and safety inspectors and helps states enforce labor laws.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan-backed bill to expand federal and state labor law enforcement died in committee without a vote, despite 65 cosponsors including 2 Republicans.
analysis.plain_summary: The Workers POWER Act would rebuild the enforcement side of the Department of Labor: more paid student internships and fellowships at the Wage and Hour Division and OSHA, doubled recent-graduate hiring, more government attorneys, retention bonuses and larger student-loan repayment to keep inspectors on the job, and $250 million a year in grants to help state labor departments hire their own enforcement staff. It would not change any worker's rights or employer penalties — it would fund the people who enforce the laws already on the books, aimed at wage theft, child labor, and workplace safety violations.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers whose wages, hours, or safety are protected by federal and state labor law — the people the Wage and Hour Division, OSHA, and state agencies are supposed to protect. The bill's findings point directly at child labor, wage and hour, and safety violations as the problem the funding would address. It also creates hiring pipelines into enforcement careers, including outreach to historically Black colleges and other minority-serving institutions.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers owed wages or working unsafe

how_it_helps.text: Requires the Labor Department to add paid student internships, double its Recent Graduates program, and add child-labor fellowship positions at the Wage and Hour Division and OSHA, plus at least 20 honors attorney positions focused on enforcement.

Creates bonus, retention, and critical-skill incentive programs for enforcement employees and raises the cap on student-loan repayment from $60,000 to $180,000, tied to a five-year service agreement, to keep experienced investigators at the Department.

Authorizes $250 million a year in competitive grants to states to hire and retain labor enforcement staff, with priority to states showing the greatest need, and requires data-sharing on repeat violators.

Directs the Labor Secretary and the Comptroller General to report to Congress on what the Department needs to enforce federal labor law, including staffing limits and partnerships with labor and community organizations.

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers, through the cost of new federal positions, bonuses, loan repayment, and the state grant program; and employers who violate wage, child-labor, or safety laws, who would face more inspections and investigations.

drawbacks.text: The bill authorizes new federal spending — $250 million a year in state grants plus new positions, bonuses, and loan repayment — without offsetting cuts, and it waives the normal certification and approval steps for bonuses, which is the kind of flexibility critics say invites loose management.

It changes no law: penalties stay the same and worker rights are unchanged, so its effect depends entirely on whether more investigators actually means more violations caught. Supporters acknowledge this by requiring a study and report on whether the added capacity is enough.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is real but modest: more inspectors cost taxpayer money, while wage theft, child labor, and safety violations cost workers billions and cost law-abiding employers who compete against violators. The bill's design is reasonable — it targets hiring, retention, and state capacity rather than new mandates — but it never got a hearing or a vote, so its actual cost and effectiveness were never tested.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Education and the Workforce Committee the day it was introduced and never received a markup, hearing, or floor vote before the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Morgan McGarvey introduced the Workers POWER Act on December 6, 2023, and it was referred to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce.

The bill drew 65 cosponsors, 63 Democrats and 2 Republicans — a level of support far above typical for legislation this session — yet the action history shows no further action after the referral to committee.

The House Education and the Workforce Committee, controlled by Republicans during the 118th Congress, never scheduled the bill for consideration, and it died at the end of the Congress on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers whose business model depends on weak enforcement of wage, child-labor, and safety laws — the industries that benefit when investigations are rare — keep the status quo. The status quo was the bill's direct target: the Wage and Hour Division and OSHA operating with staffing the bill's findings called inadequate.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers who avoid wage and safety enforcement

for.name: Rep. Morgan McGarvey
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Workers POWER Act and recruited 64 original cosponsors across both parties.

for.name: Rep. Robert C. 'Bobby' Scott of Virginia and House Democrats on Education and the Workforce
for.role: Ranking member and committee Democrats; 63 Democratic cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including the top Democrat on the committee that would have considered it.

for.name: Two House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Added bipartisan cover as 2 of the bill's 65 cosponsors.

against.name: Chair, House Committee on Education and the Workforce
against.role: Committee chair whose panel held the bill
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a committee markup or hearing; the bill's action history shows no activity after its referral to the committee.

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the House floor; it stayed in committee for the rest of the session.

sides.party_line_note: Support was heavily Democratic — 63 of 65 cosponsors — with 2 Republican cosponsors, while the Republican-led committee that controlled the bill's fate never acted on it.

industries.industry: Low-wage, labor-intensive employers (agriculture, meatpacking, fast food and franchising, warehousing)
industries.note: These are the industries where wage-and-hour, child-labor, and OSHA violations are most commonly found; more federal and state investigators mean a higher chance of getting caught and paying back wages and penalties. Weak enforcement is worth money to them, and that money is the public's — unpaid wages and unsafe conditions fall on workers.
Honest businesses are undercut by competitors who cut costs through wage theft or illegal child labor; stronger enforcement levels the field for them.

industries.industry: Labor unions and worker advocacy organizations
industries.note: The bill draws fellowship candidates from labor organizations and advocacy groups and directs the Department to report on partnerships with them, giving them a larger role in enforcement.

industries.industry: Colleges and universities, including minority-serving institutions
industries.note: The bill funds paid internships and fellowships as hiring pipelines and authorizes a competitive study grant to a higher-education institution.
